messages.author: 03bc4090a2c2b3fb
messages.subject: Understanding posterior marginals
parts:
Hi group,

I'm very new to INLA and have been running test models on data subsets and am now trying to understand how to interpret spatial patterns in my outcome, which is a count modelled with the Poisson family. From going through the various books and tutorials, I understand that to do this it is better to summarize from model$marginals.random$id.num rather than model$summary.random$id.num, but I don't understand why. I guess my confusion is that I don't understand what the marginals represent. Why can't the median of each element of model$marginals.random$id.num or model$summary.random$id.num$`0.5quant` be exponentiated to estimate the effect size for each individual spatial unit, and why does inla.emarginal(exp, marginals) gives such a different value?

I hope my question is clear! My code is below, if it helps.

Thank you in advance for your insight on this!
Pascale

> formula = culex_tarsalis_females ~ trap_type + f(id.num, model="bym", graph=sayo_w30_y2016.graph, scale.model=T)
> model = inla(formula,
+              family="poisson",
+              offset=log(trap_nights_total),
+              data=abun_over,
+              control.predictor=list(compute=T, link=1),
+              control.compute=list(dic=T, cpo=T, waic=T))

zeta = lapply(model$marginals.random$id.num[1:Nareas], function(x) inla.emarginal(exp, x))
zeta2 = data.frame(id.num=seq(1, Nareas, 1), zeta = unlist(zeta))

> # from inla.emarginal()
> summary(zeta2$zeta)
Min.     1st Qu.   Median   Mean     3rd Qu.  Max.
0.02315  0.056459  1.69461  6.04676  5.68828  133.16567

> # from summary.random
> summary(exp(model$summary.random$id.num$`0.5quant`[1:Nareas]))
Min.     1st Qu.   Median   Mean      3rd Qu.   Max.
0.02013  0.31599   0.82253  3.27497   2.74362   97.51027

> this it is better to summarize from model$marginals.random$id.num
> rather than model$summary.random$id.num, but I don't understand why.

..summary provide summaries for each marginals like E() STDEV()
quantiles etc.

the marginals densities are reported in ...marginals.random, from which
the summary statistics are computed from.

Which one you want to use, depends on what you want and need

> I guess my confusion is that I don't understand what the marginals
> represent.

its the marginals densities for each one, just plot 'x' against 'y'.



only quantiles (and not expected values) survive a monotone
transformation, like

quantile(exp(x)) = exp(quantile(x))

but

E(exp(x)) != exp(E(x))

parts:
yes, in general they are different

> r=inla(y ~ 1, data=data.frame(y=1), family="poisson")
> exp(r$summary.fixed[,"0.5quant"])
[1] 1.112208955
> inla.emarginal(exp, r$marginals.fixed$'(Intercept)')
[1] 1.518630038


you can also transform the density from 'x' to 'exp(x)' and then take
the median

> exp.intercept = inla.tmarginal(exp, r$marginals.fixed$'(Intercept)')
> inla.qmarginal(0.5, exp.intercept)
[1] 1.109500839

the difference in the result compared to 1.1122.... is due to a finite
representation of the marginal internally
